**Question:** which claims about amount, conversion, identity and purity follow
from the supplied observations—and which remain unsupported?

Allow **10 minutes**: predict for 2, change evidence for 5, then write a
restrained conclusion for 3. All observations are hypothetical teaching
scenarios; no actual isolate has been measured by this demo.

```{=html}
<section class="chem-demo" id="day25" aria-label="Integrated synthesis yield, conversion, provenance and purity claim workbench">
<p>Enable JavaScript to vary isolated mass and evidence provenance and inspect the supported claims.</p>
</section>
<script src="../interactives/core.js"></script>
<script src="../interactives/applications.js"></script>
```

### Predict

The hypothetical reaction is 1:1 with **10.00 mmol limiting reagent**, one
product per reaction extent, and product molar mass **180.16 g/mol**. Calculate
its theoretical product mass. Predict apparent isolated yield for **1.20 g**
of isolated material. Does that calculation alone provide conversion or purity?

The product is intentionally unnamed. The unassigned pattern comparison is
schematic; it is neither an aspirin measurement nor the U1 spectrum from the
other spectral demos.

### Explore

1. Vary isolated mass and keep the starting-reagent amount fixed. Notice which
   derived quantities change and which stay fixed.
2. Try the **Unrelated-spectrum trap**. Why can an apparently matching pattern
   from another teaching sample not identify this isolate?
3. Link the pattern to this isolate, then introduce an extra unexpected signal
   group. Audit identity and purity separately.
4. Compare one versus two detected TLC (thin-layer chromatography) features.
5. Supply the optional quantitative same-batch assay: **2.00 mmol starting
   material remains from 10.00 mmol initially**. Calculate conversion, then try
   the high-mass contradiction preset.

### Explain and check

Theoretical mass is $0.01000\times180.16=1.8016$ g. For 1.20 g isolated
material, apparent isolated yield is about **66.6%**, conditional on that mass
representing product. It does not measure starting-material consumption.

The optional residual assay independently gives conversion
$100(10.00-2.00)/10.00=80.0\%$. An apparent product-mass yield above this
same-batch conversion calls assumptions or records into question; retained
solvent, impurities or incompatible records are possibilities to investigate.

A consistent, explicitly linked structural observation supports an identity
claim; an unrelated trace does not. Contradictory signals require explanation.
One TLC feature does not prove purity, and two resolved features support
multiple detected components under the stated conditions.

### Model limits

The conversion assay is stipulated quantitative and linked to the same batch.
The qualitative pattern comparison supplies consistency/contradiction only;
it does not measure purity percentages or generate actual molecular spectra.
All plausible causes of a discrepancy are hypotheses, not diagnoses. Conclude
with a supported claim, a limitation and a targeted next observation, as in
[integration exercises](../integration/exercise.qmd).
